chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Vic recounts going from game-dev freelancer to agency owner to a SaaS founder at 16, and why he left project work for recurring revenue. He shares how he validates ideas, ships MVPs fast, and pivoted his product from marketers to companies.

chunks.heading: Path from game dev freelancing to an agency
chunks.text:
- Vic got into game development as a kid because he loved console gaming. His uncle worked on Watch Dogs and Assassin's Creed at Ubisoft and helped him with questions.
- He built his first simple game around age 12 or 13, then joined game-dev Discord servers and forums, helping people for free.
- His first paid gig came from a "paid work" section of a Discord server. A client paid $5 per hour and he earned roughly $75-85 in a month and a half, in seventh or eighth grade. He notes the average Romanian salary is about $800 per month, so this was meaningful money.
- He met his agency co-founders through local programming clubs and contests. They were slightly older, around 16-17, and he told them he had paid projects they could work on together.
- He started the agency "without really knowing this agency concept": he had more projects than he could code himself and took a commission by bringing in talented friends.
- He spent about two to three years on game development without real results. He says passion carried him through that period, and that being able to do the work himself meant no payroll pressure early on.

chunks.heading: Scaling the agency: channels, pricing and tech stack
chunks.text:
- Discord projects paid about $50-150, which was not enough to live on.
- To raise prices he advertised on Fiverr and did outreach to 10-15 local companies every week. Average project price rose to about $400-700 per app or website.
- He moved from games to mobile and desktop apps because companies would pay for them.
- Stack: Capacitor JS for iOS and Android, Electron JS for desktop, all JavaScript. A common job was a Windows-only app that the client wanted on Mac and Linux, so they recoded it natively.
- Client sources were SEO, Fiverr, Upwork, Guru, and outbound.
- Notable clients: a listed Swiss mechanical-parts company (conference slideshow software, hired through its manager on a tight deadline), a European jersey store, and gaming YouTuber Super Shiftery (150-200k subscribers).
- Revenue was seasonal. Summer was the peak because companies build products and features then, ahead of the late-fall marketing season.
- Total agency revenue reached "five to six figures."

chunks.heading: Why he left the agency for SaaS
chunks.text:
He gave three reasons:
- Revenue was declining month over month, and no-code tools for desktop, mobile and web apps were rising.
- Software development agency work has no recurring revenue: clients pay for one project, and only small updates or maintenance follow.
- His co-founders had exams, college and internships, and he had stopped enjoying the calls and project management.

He treated the agency as a stepping stone toward a subscription company. He finished existing projects, slowed client work, and brainstormed and tested SaaS ideas on the market until one became profitable. The transition was smooth.

chunks.heading: Validating a SaaS idea before building
chunks.text:
- Put up a quick landing page (WordPress, Webflow or Bubble) with a mockup image and a hook that states the problem or solution, plus an email collection field.
- Do outreach to about 100 people on LinkedIn or Twitter and talk to people in communities like Indie Hackers. Perhaps 10 reply, but expert opinions count ten times more than friends and parents saying it's a great idea.
- Then pick the tech stack that gets an MVP out fastest, because fast shipping lets you iterate.
- Example: Fistash started targeting affiliate marketers and had to flip to companies. Because it was built fast, the pivot was cheap.
- Without coding skills he suggests no-code tools: Webflow, Bubble, Zapier, with Gumroad, Paddle or Stripe for payments.

chunks.heading: Fistash: how he found the problem and how it works
chunks.text:
- Fistash helps companies and startups find and recruit affiliates and partners using AI. It started in January 2023.
- The pivot: he first built it for affiliate marketers to find products. Advisors in the industry told him businesses have more revenue and capital than marketers, so he flipped it to target companies.
- The problem came from his own agency days. He wanted people who could resell his services for commission and found no efficient, affordable way to do it.
- Companies pay affiliate or partnership managers to do repetitive work: collect affiliates in a spreadsheet and reach out manually. He cites that 84% of US companies have an affiliate program.
- Two sides:
  - An AI-powered marketplace where affiliates sign up and apply to programs. They get two daily software offers with content to start promoting.
  - A custom AI search engine his team built from agency experience. It scrapes social platforms and the web, and returns contact details and traffic numbers.
- The base plan gives 150 affiliate leads from a form the company fills in at signup.
- Why software for affiliates: recurring revenue, the same thing he missed in the agency.
- Stack: JavaScript with Next.js for the app and landing page, and a Python API. He built it in two weeks with a friend from the agency, with whom he had good chemistry.

chunks.heading: Growth numbers, the acquisition offer and exit plans
chunks.text:
- MRR: $110 in month one, about doubled in month two, and crossed $500 in month three.
- At about two and a half months, with MRR around $380-480, a company known in the affiliate space offered about $35,000.
- He rejected it because MRR was growing 50-100% every month, so he thought it was undervalued. He projected over $1,000 MRR in six months. He stays in touch with that company, and they have sent him referrals and customers.
- He hired a commission-based CMO because he describes himself as "really bad at sales, marketing", so he can focus on product and AI matching accuracy.
- Goals: $5-6k MRR in about a year and a possible exit above $400,000 later. If it doesn't work, he would rethink strategy or pivot.

chunks.heading: Twitter, AI and handling setbacks
chunks.text:
- He returned to Twitter at the start of 2023 with a goal: sell the product and connect with people. He observed that big SaaS founders get promotion for their companies through personal brand.
- On AI, he argues there are many niche problems that automation or AI can solve right now. His example is the story-sync app Story Heap, built by a Romanian entrepreneur at 17, which reposted Snapchat stories to Instagram and Facebook and reached $1M in sales in six months. He describes the lesson as finding a repetitive manual task, automating it, and making an offer companies can't refuse.
- On churn: think about what happens if you 100x the company, since then you'll have hundreds of churned customers every month. So get used to it, and talk to churned customers to understand why instead of making excuses.
- He ends his days by writing three things he's grateful for.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Vic, a 17-year-old founder and ex-agency owner, explains how he validated Affistash by calling affiliate managers before writing code, then automated the manual partner-discovery work with AI. He shares early-founder lessons on idea validation, mentors, mockups and picking a niche you enjoy.

chunks.heading: Validating before building
chunks.text:
- Vic says to "validate your idea and your concept before you start building it" and that he tells every entrepreneur he meets the same thing. He picked the habit up at his software development agency, where founders always validated before the agency built.
- For Affistash (affiliate recruitment software), he cold-messaged affiliate managers in affiliate marketing communities, subreddits and on LinkedIn.
- His pitch: he is an ex software-agency founder building something in their space, and asks what feedback they have and what product would make their life easier.
- He asked each manager to walk through their whole process, from starting an affiliate program to landing the first affiliates and partners and managing them.
- The research took about two to three weeks of calls with affiliate managers. Some of those managers became customers once the tool was built.
- Findings: recruitment and partner lead discovery were entirely manual (paying for SEO tools, checking who promotes competitors, scouting leads, judging fit). Finding 5 to 10 prospects could take hours, which made it a good fit for AI.

chunks.heading: Low-fidelity validation with a mockup deck
chunks.text:
- Vic's process for every product or business: build a mockup or very low-level demo, even a quick deck in Canva or Figma. You don't need to be a pro designer or developer.
- Write to people in your industry and ask for 5 to 10 minutes on a call, then show them the deck.
- He says many people want to help in the early stage, and you can get roughly 10 to 20 opinions this way.
- You don't have to ask for payment up front. Offer a free account once the product is built as thanks for the feedback.

chunks.heading: Networks, mentors and picking a niche
chunks.text:
- Vic resonates with "your network is your net worth". He says to surround yourself with the biggest, most influential people in your niche, because they help when you expand to new markets and industries and their referrals can mean a lot.
- A good network also means always having someone to consult before a business decision. He has two or three mentors he speaks to before any new venture or major decision.
- His mentors are SaaS founders with hundreds of thousands of dollars in MRR and seven-figure exits.
- He argues young founders have a better chance of connecting with such people, because many successful entrepreneurs started young and see themselves in them.
- His third lesson: work in a niche you are passionate about, because it keeps you motivated through the tough stretches (angry customers, lots of demos and meetings). He is passionate about AI and automation, so building an automation tool made sense.

chunks.heading: What Affistash does and who it targets
chunks.text:
- Target user: affiliate managers and partner managers whose main task includes recruiting new affiliates and publishers.
- Customer mix: about 70 to 80% SaaS, mostly small and medium B2C SaaS companies with roughly 5 to 15 employees. The rest are e-commerce and info products. He chose SaaS because it is the industry he knows best, which made it easier to reach founders and managers there.
- B2C SaaS fits because those companies advertise heavily through publishers and content creators.
- He was starting to expand into enterprise teams with established affiliate recruitment and partnership departments, and had begun working with a few affiliate management teams at bigger companies.
- Core feature: AI-driven partner lead discovery. The user fills in company data (name, niche, website, business model, product description, target audience). The tool then generates leads for chosen partner types: content creators, media publishers, agencies, newsletters, or a mix.
- Platform options include SEO (top-ranked content for the niche and target audience), YouTube, LinkedIn and Twitter.
- Demo example: for a SaaS product (Sofa Brain) targeting interior designers and real estate agents, the tool generated 112 publisher leads automatically, such as "top 10 AI tools for interior design" lists monetized with AdSense and affiliate links.
- Leads can be refreshed by choosing a new type and platform and giving feedback.
- Each lead can pull contacts (email, LinkedIn, Twitter) and shows an accuracy percentage so managers can tell which are better fits.
- Outreach happens in the tool: connect a mailbox, then use an AI template library with selectable writing styles and word limits. Templates are generated from your company data.
- He advises personalizing every email because it improves conversion rates.

chunks.heading: Where the lead data comes from
chunks.text:
- Vic says leads come from a mix of sources: a database of manually collected leads built by the Affistash team, plus scraping APIs and scrapers connected to specific platforms and networks (YouTube, LinkedIn, Twitter and others).
- The thesis behind the product: the AI can run the searches, grab and classify leads, filter them, and generate outreach messages far faster than a manager doing it by hand.

chunks.heading: Pricing at the time of the interview
chunks.text:
- Individual (premium) plan: $37 per month billed annually, $47 per month billed monthly. Aimed at solo affiliate managers and freelancers, covers one company profile.
- Enterprise plan: $128+ per month billed annually, $257 per month billed monthly. Includes five team accounts and the ability to recruit partners for multiple affiliate programs, so it suits agencies and recruitment agencies working with several clients.
- He said they were still testing the market and were new, that pricing would likely change within months, and that he agreed they were underpriced given how expensive tools are in the industry.

chunks.heading: Where affiliate management and AI are heading
chunks.text:
- Vic expects a lot of automation and AI in affiliate management. Recruitment is only one step of a successful program.
- Other areas he sees AI improving: onboarding (generating content and tools for partners and having conversations with them), commission optimization and data analysis.
- He also sees real-time interaction with partners during onboarding, for example an AI changing banner colors to match a partner's website theme.
- On the content side, he expects people to create far more affiliate content with AI (video, niche blogs) and an array of AI tools and AI-produced content in the industry.
- He described "endless possibilities" for AI and automation here and suggested AI banner generation for affiliates as a business idea.

chunks.heading: Early-stage habits
chunks.text:
- Vic ran a software development agency before Affistash, building desktop and game software for companies, including enterprise-sized ones. Agency work relied on partnerships and referral commissions, which introduced him to affiliate and partnership marketing.
- He started Affistash at the beginning of 2023, with a co-founder, while still in high school, and held demos around his school schedule.
- He researched competitors' landing pages (for example, looking at what managers like to see) when redesigning his own landing page, often late at night.
- To stay visible he posts regularly on LinkedIn, shares demos weekly for B2B SaaS, AI SaaS and e-commerce companies, and offers tailored live demos with partner leads already loaded for a prospect's company.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Vic Giurgiu demos Affistash, an AI tool he built for affiliate managers that matches a company with publishers, creators and agencies, pulls contacts, and drafts outreach emails. He explains the design logic (one-input setup, feedback loop, manual plus automated search) and the pricing.

chunks.heading: How Affistash works: AI matching from company data to partner leads
chunks.text:
Vic built Affistash (the product is also called "FS" / Affy stash in the transcript) in early 2023 as an AI tool for affiliate managers. He started by chatting with a few affiliate managers to find "the best idea and the best tool that can be built specifically for affiliate managers using the power of AI." The tool recruits affiliates, publishers and partners for one or more affiliate programs.

- The user inputs company data once: name, niche, website, business model, geolocation, price range, subscription model (one time, recurring, per usage) and a short description.
- The algorithm uses this to understand what the company does and who its ideal affiliates are.
- Vic's demo company was "Sofa Brain", an AI SaaS for interior designers and real estate agents.
- A business can run recruitment for multiple affiliate programs from one dashboard.

chunks.heading: Discovery: partner types, match rate and the feedback loop
chunks.text:
- Partner types searchable: affiliate partners (a mix of everything), content creators, blog/media publishers (SEO), agencies and newsletters. Each type supports a different set of platforms.
- Each lead shows a sample post, a partner type classification and a match rate estimated by the AI. A higher match rate means a better fit.
- The demo surfaced "top 10 AI interior design tools" listicles and "AI for real estate agents" articles, publishers already ranking in search and monetizing with AdSense and affiliate links.
- Each lead has a "get contacts" button returning email plus LinkedIn (and Twitter), so outreach can happen on more than one channel.
- Up/down votes train the algorithm. Upvoting a publisher returns more leads like it (e.g. housing.com); downvoting teaches it to avoid that type of partner.
- Refreshing opens a feedback pop-up (what you liked and didn't like), and a new lead list arrives in about two to three minutes. His demo refresh returned 112 leads.
- Leads can be exported as CSV or shared with teammates by email.
- The more the platform is used, the better the results get.

chunks.heading: Outreach: AI email templates and recruitment campaigns
chunks.text:
- Users connect their mailbox and run recruitment campaigns inside the tool. It tracks emails sent and emails that failed to deliver.
- An AI template library composes outreach using the company data already entered and the details known about the publisher. Options include style (e.g. casual) and length (e.g. under 100 words).
- Vic recommends personalizing each message for the specific partner: it "obviously results in way better open rates, way better conversion rates." The AI template is meant to get you the first draft so you "move way faster."
- Replies land in the user's own mailbox, so conversations continue there.

chunks.heading: Manual partner search engine
chunks.text:
- Besides automated matching, Affistash has a manual search where the user enters their own short or long keywords, similar to tools like Gro/"roia"-style SEO partner finders (the name is unclear in the transcript).
- It also searches social and B2B platforms such as LinkedIn and Telegram (to find communities), not only SEO results.
- Vic positions it as a way to get even more leads than the automated engine finds.

chunks.heading: Pricing and packaging
chunks.text:
- Individual affiliate managers: 450 leads per month for $47/month on the monthly plan, or $37/month on the annual plan.
- Enterprise plan for teams: more than 1,000 leads per month and 6 dashboard seats, at $257/month, or $128/month on the annual plan.
- Vic's argument: price per lead is low because the discovery and outreach are automated.
- Product design choices: contextual help text on features, a live demo in the dashboard for teammates, and "talk to an expert" buttons at setup steps so the team can assist customers.

chunks.heading: Roadmap
chunks.text:
- Next planned feature: AI-assisted onboarding of new partners and handling onboarding conversations, once the AI is "well enough trained."
- Stated goal: automate as much of the recruitment process as possible, from discovering new partner leads to outreaching them and closing partnerships "as fast as possible."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Vic Giurgiu walks through the most time-consuming affiliate manager tasks (recruitment, email outreach, fake-follower checks, onboarding) and the AI tools he uses for each. He also shares how a teen founder balances school and building, and why outsourcing and growth-first thinking matter.

chunks.heading: Affiliate recruitment with AppyStash: turning a brand URL into a prospect list
chunks.text:
- Vic co-builds AppyStash with Dustin Howes, a tool that turns a brand's URL into a list of potential affiliates and influencers using AI, machine learning and automation.
- Workflow: enter the brand URL, the platform extracts keywords, target audience and description, then you open "Discover partners" and pick a discovery method.
- His favorite method is the "AI Partner Finder": select the partner type and platform. It supports open 10 platforms and, he believes, is probably the only tool that searches affiliates and influencers on social platforms as well as the open web.
- Example: for an e-commerce flower brand it returned posts ranking for the brand's own top keywords, so there is no separate keyword analysis and no expensive SEO tool needed. Each result also shows traffic data, top keywords and geographic data.
- "Lookalike" search: pick a platform (SEO, YouTube, Twitter and so on) and it finds hundreds of similar affiliates posting on the same keywords. Dustin calls it the feature he uses almost daily to replicate a good affiliate.

chunks.heading: Building a YouTuber lead list with email and affiliate-link signals in under five minutes
chunks.text:
Vic's process for the 800-YouTuber lead list:

1. Open the manual search engine and choose YouTube.
2. Add multiple "keywords to include", for example "best products for better sleep" and "sleep product review". Advanced filters allow excluded keywords and hashtags on social platforms.
3. Search (the demo returned 150 results of quality publishers ranking for those queries).
4. Click export. A CSV arrives by email after a couple of minutes.

- The export includes source, contact URL, contact email (scraped from public channel descriptions) and the referral link.
- Referral links are a buying-intent signal: Genius Link, ShareASale, Amazon and bit.ly links "highly indicate affiliate activity".
- Not every YouTuber has a public email, so sort A to Z to put leads with emails first and leave the rest for manual outreach.
- He says the whole list takes under five minutes.
- Dustin adds that clicking through YouTube to find emails behind a captcha is the annoying part this skips.

chunks.heading: AI-personalized cold outreach to affiliate prospects
chunks.text:
- Vic recommends Instantly (used internally, "worked really well") and Smartlead for bulk affiliate outreach; both are affordable.
- Tactic: put a content example (e.g. the prospect's video title) into a custom variable and have a GPT prompt write an icebreaker complimenting that video.
- Example output: "I saw you have a video about fast and efficient car chargers, that's funny because I was just looking for one for my new car."
- Why it works: it reads far better than a generic bulk email ("join my affiliate program", "can you review this product"), and signals that their content already helped someone and that there is money to be made.

chunks.heading: Spotting fake followers with HypeAuditor before spending on influencers
chunks.text:
- Vic calls fake followers a big problem in influencer marketing, and posted a LinkedIn carousel about it that people liked.
- He recommends HypeAuditor's free "check any influencer" feature.
- What to read:
  - Engagement rate, compared to the industry standard for that channel.
  - Subscriber growth chart: a sharp spike followed by much slower growth can mean bought followers or views, or can just be a viral video, so check which.
  - Total video views and average views.
- He demoed it on MKBHD and Marques Brownlee's channel; AppyStash also shows views, likes and audience interests when you fetch audience data.

chunks.heading: Onboarding new affiliates: email sequences and an AI support bot
chunks.text:
- A new affiliate should enter an onboarding email sequence. Vic suggests MailerLite (very cheap and affordable) or Mailchimp for a more enterprise solution.
- Three things to cover: emails, onboarding materials and affiliate support.
- Boost Box (built by Ru from Australia, a community member, early stage) lets you train a chatbot on your materials, past affiliate work and policies, so affiliates ask the AI first and escalate to the manager or support team only if needed.
- Benefit: removes repetitive support emails from the manager's inbox.
- Dustin adds a caveat that partnership marketing must not lose face-to-face relationship building.

chunks.heading: Staying productive as a teen founder: AI leverage, outsourcing and avoiding burnout
chunks.text:
- AI is what lets Vic ship features, launch new products and fix bugs fast while in high school; he says he didn't realize how much it helps until asked.
- He is cautious about burnout at 16 to 18, calling it among the unhealthiest things that can happen, and says to zoom out ("where we were a year ago or two years ago") on bad sales or feedback days.
- Advice for young founders:
  - Early on, focus on growth over profitability.
  - Outsource as much as you can: pay someone to run social media or implement a feature if the budget allows.
  - Build a quality team; he likes working with people around his own age.
  - Take advantage of low expenses while living with parents or newly moved out.
  - Travel and take breaks to keep balance.
  - Learning business fundamentals early is valuable even if the business is not doing big numbers, and the right people will join for part-time pay or for free to be part of a bigger mission.
- He also built Podkit, a media kit tool for podcasters, finished that month.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Vic's personal yearly essay covering 2025: scaling Affistash past $6K MRR, launching and selling PodKit to Listener.com, exiting Affistash to FMTC, and joining the ClujHouse builder community. Mostly narrative, with reflections on money, purpose, and why he builds.

chunks.heading: Business trajectory and timeline in 2025
chunks.text:
- Vic started 2025 after what he calls "the success of 2024", with Affistash at $4,000 MRR in January.
- Affistash reached $6,000 MRR by March.
- In March he also signed a $1,300 MRR customer for a lead generation subscription tool he built in stealth. He tweeted about it, which sparked the discussion that led to his first acquisition of the year.
- He launched PodKit (a media kit tool for podcasters) in February and had revenue the same week.
- In April he sold PodKit to Listener.com and joined as founding member and Head of Engineering (role started in July).
- In late November he sold Affistash to FMTC. He calls it life-changing, though "far from an amount that would set me up for retirement."
- By the end of the year he describes his investment portfolio at a 55% rate of return.

chunks.heading: How PodKit started: partnering through a warm intro
chunks.text:
- Vic's Affistash co-founder Dustin introduced him to Eric, who owns a B2B podcast network (B2B Pod Pros) and works with podcasters.
- The pitch was simply "why don't you work together on PodKit?" Vic said yes.
- Eric became co-founder on PodKit.
- The tool launched in February and had revenue within the same week.
- Takeaway Vic implies: a partner with direct access to the target customer (podcasters) shortens the path to first revenue.

chunks.heading: Selling PodKit and joining the acquirer
chunks.text:
- Casey Adams of Listener.com messaged Vic about potentially acquiring PodKit. Vic was at a party when the message came in.
- He sold PodKit in April, only about two months after launch, and joined Listener's team as founding member and Head of Engineering.
- He values the learning from working alongside people he admires (Casey Adams, Kieran O'Brien).
- Work at Listener included a Megaphone integration (built partly while on a family vacation in Greece) and a big product launch in December.
- Listener is changing its market positioning in 2026 after that launch, which he sees as large growth potential.

chunks.heading: Exiting Affistash
chunks.text:
- In August, while on vacation, Vic started thinking about exiting Affistash, his most profitable business to date.
- Affistash was co-founded with Dustin.
- He sold it to FMTC at the end of November.
- Effect on him: more confidence in his "building capabilities" and readiness to "do things bigger and better than ever."
- He celebrated by taking his best friends to dinner.

chunks.heading: Community and surrounding yourself with builders
chunks.text:
- A Twitter DM from Andrei (Bantu) in February led him to ClujHouse, a place for young people in Romania to build together. Before it, he felt "alone" in his interest in startups, with only David and Alex to talk shop with.
- He describes ClujHouse as a "brotherhood" or "fellowship" he had been seeking for a while.
- The space moved from a corporate office to a mansion in downtown Cluj and joined the LocalhostHQ network, which brought introductions to people like Kei and Hardeep.
- Months later, he and his ClujHouse friends were each in better positions with their businesses than ever.

chunks.heading: Mindset: money, mortality and the drive to create
chunks.text:
- A shoulder skin surgery and a two-week cancer scare in November (it turned out to be a skin infection) changed how he views life.
- He says he does not want the mentality he had at 16-17, "chasing money and thinking that would somehow make everyone love me."
- On ambition: "the higher I get, the more I want to climb," and he accepts and embraces that.
- He concludes that "the purpose of my life is to create": whether an idea succeeds or fails, he feels the need to bring it into the world, the same feeling since his first YouTube video at age 11.
- He treats the work-life balance practically: he kept working 6-8 hours a day while travelling, and notes the exhaustion of pairing that with heavy nightlife.
- Using money well: he did charity with friends at Christmas and calls it "genuinely one of the best things money can do."

chunks.heading: 2025 outputs and plans for 2026
chunks.text:
- He launched GameCap, his first open source project, and wants to do more open source work.
- He started apartment shopping to buy his first property and move out early in 2026, funded by the year's business growth.
- He is studying AI at UBB Cluj but does the bare minimum, because the degree competes with focusing on the work where he makes his money.
- For 2026 he is "more hungry than ever to build something big" and aims to grow his role at Listener.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Vic's personal year-in-review as an 18-year-old software founder. He recounts growing Affistash with an audience co-founder, the marketing channels that moved revenue, a quick SaaS exit via Twitter, and the anxiety and relationship lessons behind the business growth.

chunks.heading: Building Affistash in 2024: growth from marketing and a co-founder
chunks.text:
- Vic started 2024 by finding an "audience co-founder" for Affistash, a product he almost sold in 2023 ("so happy i didnt").
- The co-founder handled marketing work and revenue began growing, which fueled Vic's motivation to keep building software.
- First time crossing $2.5k MRR came in Q2.
- By autumn, income grew a lot from reinvested marketing money, and Vic started thinking about delegating and automating more marketing tasks.
- His year-end screenshot showed Affistash MRR up 442.4% versus the previous year.
- He still felt "hungrier, and more pressured than ever", partly because other people now depended on the project.
- Stated goal for 2025: reach "6 figs recurring".

chunks.heading: Affistash marketing tactics that worked in fall 2024
chunks.text:
- **pSEO:** Vic wrote a Python script plus Framer CMS to index 5000 pages.
- **Cold email:** bought 6 mailboxes and got around a 15% reply rate, which he called "insane". Automating the reply process was still in progress.
- **LinkedIn and YouTube content:** he and his co-founder took LinkedIn content more seriously, and views grew noticeably.
- **Conferences:** the co-founder attended a few, which resulted in bigger deals.
- **Landing page:** moved from NextJS to Framer, and conversion rates "improved a lot".
- **Onboarding:** improved the onboarding process and started collecting more data about users and where they come from.

chunks.heading: Selling a SaaS via a single tweet: Coverposts exit
chunks.text:
- In summer 2024 Vic sold coverposts.com, a social media marketing tool built with @ditu_dev. It was his first SaaS exit of the year.
- The process was simple: post a tweet (it went semi-viral), receive 10-15 DMs from interested buyers, and sell to a CTO based in California.
- Distribution via his Twitter audience did the work of finding buyers. He reached 1000 followers in Jan 2024.

chunks.heading: Developmently's business model and side experiments
chunks.text:
- Vic runs a software company called Developmently. The main revenue model is building and selling its own SaaS products.
- In 2024 he gave the service model another try after almost a year and a half of stopping it: backend development and consultancy gigs with a designer/frontend developer friend.
- By late summer he had signed a couple of big clients for software dev services.
- A community marketing database, trygrouphunt.com, built with @ditu_dev, "failed lol".
- He considered starting a water labeling company with a friend and is keeping the idea to himself for now.
- In December he started building a new software product, with the outcome left for his 2025 essay.

chunks.heading: Motivation and mindset behind building
chunks.text:
- The year began with "a new found motivation to build cool shit, with no expectations or intentions to please anybody".
- He never started with the goal of making money; the current situation feels "surreal".
- He values running an online business from anywhere in the world at a young age.
- Anxiety was his biggest demon: "a lot of second guessing, fear of losing and anxiety" since he started business at 13-14.
- He felt "always in a hurry" and workaholic, even when business and school were going well.
- "Money doesnt mean shit": losing relationships with people he cares about is "1000x more painful than any customer dispute, any churn or any lost money". He still chases revenue.
- Writing the yearly essay worked as therapy, and he plans to make it recurring.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Vic's personal homepage lists his track record: indie games, a dev agency turned software studio, and several products built and sold (Affistash, BrowserUnicorn, Coverposts, PodKit). He is open about failed products too. It is a bio, not a how-to, so it offers little tactical insight.

chunks.heading: Origin: from a $75 game dev gig to shipping software
chunks.text:
- At 13, Vic made $75 from a game dev gig, which he says changed his life.
- He studies AI in college and builds software companies.
- His early path: launched 2 indie games that reached over 2,000 players, then ran a software dev agency with his closest friends and built products for IPOs.
- He turned the agency into a software studio and launched SaaS products. In his words, "Some were successful, some were not."

chunks.heading: Exits and wins
chunks.text:
- **Affistash:** grew it to 6 figures at 17 with a co-founder (Dustin Howes), then sold it to FMTC at 19.
- **BrowserUnicorn:** built and sold it with a partner (@ditu_dev), and listed it on Product Hunt.
- **Coverposts.com:** built and sold with the same partner.
- **PodKit:** built and sold in 3 months to listener.com, working with Eric Melchor.
- Also won hackathon awards with Dialz.

chunks.heading: Pattern: build small products with partners and sell them
chunks.text:
- Most of his listed outcomes are small products built with a co-founder and sold, rather than long-held companies.
- PodKit shows the speed of this approach: build to sale in 3 months.
- The agency and studio served as the base: client work first, then the studio launching its own SaaS products.

chunks.heading: Failed products
chunks.text:
Vic openly lists what didn't work:

- **linklyft:** link in bio for freelancers.
- **grouphunt:** a community marketing tool.
- **characterstream:** FaceTime-like interactions with AI characters.
- **gitwall:** paywalls on GitHub repos.
- **browzy:** a productivity Chrome extension.

His stance: ship many products, publish the failures next to the wins, and treat both as part of the record.

chunks.heading: Documenting the journey
chunks.text:
- He writes yearly essays documenting his life and travels (2024, 2025).
- He keeps a public presence through his site, vic.ceo, and posts on Twitter/X.
- He invites people to reach out by email if he can be helpful.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Third-person write-up of a podcast interview with Vic about building Affistash, an AI affiliate recruitment tool, as a teenager. Covers validating the idea through community engagement, choosing a passionate niche, networking and mentorship, and where automation is taking affiliate marketing. Vic's own words are paraphrased, not quoted.

chunks.heading: Affistash: what it is and who it's for
chunks.text:
- Vic built Affistash (also written "Afstache" in the episode notes) as affiliate recruitment software that automates lead discovery for affiliate and partner managers.
- Target user: affiliate and partner managers, particularly in the SaaS industry.
- He started working at an affiliate marketing agency at 15 and was 17 when he built and launched Affistash while still in high school.
- The name is tied to the affiliate industry itself.
- Core promise: take the manual work out of finding partners. Instead of hunting for affiliates by hand, a manager gets a list of relevant, contactable partners.

chunks.heading: How the product works
chunks.text:
- The dashboard shows stats, educational demos and a list of discovered leads.
- AI-driven partner discovery generates leads for different partner types, from content creators to media publishers.
- Each lead comes with contact details such as email and LinkedIn.
- Users connect their own mailbox and send outreach from inside the tool, using AI-generated email templates tailored to the partner type.
- Data sources are a mix of a manually collected database and APIs/scrapers for platforms like YouTube, LinkedIn and Twitter.
- Vic offers personalized demos to people who reach out.

chunks.heading: Validating the idea before building
chunks.text:
- Vic's research approach was to validate Affistash as an affiliate recruitment tool through community engagement, talking to the people who would use it rather than assuming demand.
- He stresses idea validation as the first step, ahead of building.
- He credits networking and mentorship as major factors in getting a product to market as a teenager.
- He advises picking a niche you are passionate about, since the work of refining the product is long and sustained.

chunks.heading: Pricing
chunks.text:
- Plans are built to be affordable and flexible, from individual marketers up to enterprise teams.
- The enterprise plan is aimed at teams running multiple affiliate programs.
- The interviewer's reaction was that the pricing is low and the tool may be underpriced for the value it delivers. That is the host's view, not Vic's.

chunks.heading: Where Vic sees affiliate marketing going
chunks.text:
- He expects more automation and AI across the affiliate workflow.
- The areas he expects to be optimized first are recruitment, onboarding and commission processing.
- Affistash's role is to move recruitment from manual prospecting toward automated, AI-assisted discovery and outreach.

chunks.heading: Work ethic and shipping habits
chunks.text:
- Vic worked late at night to redesign the Affistash landing page, and defends that as part of continually refining and improving the product for affiliate managers.
- He balances running the business with school, treating the product as something that needs ongoing iteration rather than a one-time launch.

chunks.heading: Distribution tactics for outreach
chunks.text:
- The interview's advice to managers is to connect with prospects on LinkedIn alongside email, and to use AI-generated templates to speed up outreach. Vic's product is built around that combined contact-plus-template workflow.
- He offers personalized demos and invites direct engagement on LinkedIn and Twitter as a way to reach his own buyers.

Something I’ve been thinking about lately:

How many talented people had their spirit crushed by school before they ever got to see what they could actually build?

I ask because even now, I still feel anxious when a professor critiques one of my assignments.

Or when I fail an exam.

Not disappointed.

Actually anxious.

Which feels strange when I zoom out.

I’ve written apps myself that generated hundreds of thousands of dollars.

Fully written by me.

For my own companies.

For clients.

Some of them were used by thousands of people, including people working at companies like Puma, Surfshark, Amazon, and others.

And yet somehow, a university assignment can still make me feel like I’m not “good enough.”

That’s what worries me.

Because I at least have some real-world proof to fall back on.

I can remind myself:

“I’ve built things people use.”

“I’ve built things people paid for.”

“This grade is not the full picture.”

But what about the person who doesn’t have that yet?

The student who hasn’t built a product.

The developer who hasn’t had a client.

The kid who is still trying to believe they might be good at this.

What happens when the only mirror they have is school?

And that mirror keeps telling them they’re not enough?

In the real world, the feedback loop is different.

You build something.

People use it.

Someone pays for it.

It works, or it doesn’t.

But in school, a failed exam or a harsh critique can hit some old part of your brain that says:

“Maybe I’m just not that good.”

And if you hear that enough times before you have any counter-evidence, I can see how it could genuinely crush your spirit.

Not because you’re incapable.

But because the system made you confuse performance in school with potential in life.

I don’t really have a clean conclusion.

Just this uncomfortable thought:

Maybe a lot of people don’t quit because they lack talent.

Maybe they quit because the only system they trusted convinced them too early that they didn’t have any.

Curious if other builders, developers, students, or dropouts feel this too:

How much potential do you think gets lost because school becomes the only mirror people use to judge themselves?
